title: Narrative and worldbuilding
thesis: In a roguelike the story players remember is mostly one they assemble themselves from systems, fragments and failures, so the designer's job is less to tell a story than to build a world that generates, implies and acknowledges stories, and to make fiction and mechanics say the same thing. Authored narrative still has a place, but only when it is shaped for repetition and death (braided, gated, brief, optional) and when the numbers, symbols and tone underneath it are chosen deliberately.

sections.heading: Where roguelike stories come from
sections.brief: Open with the chapter's foundation: games carry embedded (authored) and emergent (player-made) stories, and several speakers independently claim roguelikes are unusually good at the second kind (Lazer-Walker, Kreminski, Tarn Adams, Brian Walker on Brogue's co-authored path, Shepard on Dungeonmans' near-plotless tone). Show the convergence that players retell what systems did, not scripted beats (Adams' buckets vs. boss fights, Reed on The Hobbit's simulationist 'bugs' resurfacing in roguelikes, Brittain's hand stuck in a pot in Shiren, Cummings' baseball as story engine), and that retelling is the evidence a generator worked (Smith Nicholls). Then cover the raw ingredients: chaos (Clark), dice that redirect (Main), player mistakes (Heat Signature), other players (Plummer), and happy accidents of naming in Blaseball and of glitches in Pokemon Glitch (Rabii's authorless story). End with guidance on what a designer must provide for emergence: interlocking, consistent, investigable systems (Adams) plus room for players to fill in.

sections.heading: Let the player's imagination do the work
sections.brief: Argue that sparse presentation is a strength: Rogue's creators found letters and stats were enough because players imagined the rest, and Hewitt, Compton, Capacle and Freeman converge on apophenia and pattern-seeking turning thin stimuli into stories. Then move to the practical consequence that story should be given in fragments and gaps (Paul Dean on non-linear and fragmentary lore and on introducing ideas without explaining them, Mike Cook on cropped item descriptions, coined vocabulary in La Horde du Contrevent and Qud, NetHack's false rumors as near-free possibility). Use Keenan's Duskers shuffling experiments to show order changes interpretation. Close with immersion versus frame: Grinblat's frame analysis says players never fully forget they are at a computer and Carney prefers resonance to immersion; set these against Hewitt's knowing-cooperation view. End with guidance: show less, leave hooks, write authored content that stays meaningful whatever the world turns out to be (Lazer-Walker).

sections.heading: Players as co-authors
sections.brief: Lead with Kreminski's frame that games are storytelling partners which help players past creative barriers (blank canvas, judgment, writer's block, perfectionism) through generativity, incrementality, boundedness and limited options; this is the section's spine. Converge it with Reed's point that remembered and called-back small choices create ownership, Wehrle's Oath which generates meaning in the post-game report and ships a journal, the 2018 panel idea of a player-written death blurb, Grinblat's reparative play, and Otto's tarot-style reader-as-player. Bring in Junius on theatre: a script is finished by its production, just as players finish a run, and his reading of Hades as rehearsal toward opening night. Include co-creative tools (Cozy Mystery Construction Kit transcripts, rewritable NPC lines in Reality Break, map-drawing games like The Quiet Year) and the authorship question (Grinblat via Emily Short). End with concrete levers a designer can pull to make players better storytellers.

sections.heading: Story shapes that fit a roguelike
sections.brief: Argue that roguelikes suit particular narrative forms: short self-contained adventures and the picaresque rather than the epic (Brough on short stories, Cugel and Vancian loadouts), stories about systems and societies rather than one chosen hero (Uduwana), and rogues acting from self-interest rather than destiny (Darren Grey, the murder-hobo). Set Brittain's critique of prescriptive story structure and happy-ending bias, and Cedotal's point about overwhelming options as the modern anxiety, against Brittain's own defence of the power fantasy. Cover what the run structure allows: failure without dissonance, rotating protagonists, vignettes, Rashomon-like unreliable narrators that no game has yet done. Contrast structure: Tarn Adams finds adventure mode flat without overarching structure and proposes villains' schemes as plot, Carney's 'pulse' of descent gives coherence, while Lazer-Walker and Wehrle abandon shaped endings and Keenan learned players wanted a definitive resolution. End with guidance for choosing a story shape that matches run length and death.

sections.heading: Death, restarts and the loop as narrative
sections.brief: Start with the decision every narrative roguelike faces: whether and how to justify restarting. Early games gave no reason; Hades and Cobalt Core build it into the lore (Cartlidge/Dolgin/Tomlinson, Solomons), and Dolgin argues comedy can skip the justification while serious tone demands it. Then the costs of story under repetition: replayed intros become a burden (Keenan, Aversa), dramatic story and replayable systems remain hard to reconcile (Wilson on Prey: Mooncrash), and strong attachment can make permadeath unbearable (Lisa Brown) — set these against Stella Vermilion-style attachment elsewhere if useful. Develop Solomons' hauntology (Returnal, Inscryption death cards, places stained by failure, reloads as possession) and loops as theme (The Void Rains Upon Her Heart). Then the persistence toolkit: meta presence and metaprogression as storytelling (Shepard's Joppa idea, nemesis dungeons, Biskup's persistent legends), Duskers keeping logs across deaths, lineage as in Darkest Dungeon, and death screens, messages and chronologies (Dredmor vs. Qud). End with practical options for making death meaningful in the fiction.

sections.heading: When fiction and mechanics pull together
sections.brief: Open with Keenan's diagnosis that curated story is disliked when it is not integrated with the roguelike structure, and Kim's 'subjective simulation' in The Shrouded Isle, where the cult's values are the resources so players embrace them; these and Shepard's call to put the player at the centre of events through play converge. Then show fiction selling mechanics: Against the Storm's impatient queen, Party House's ban, Pacific Drive's fuel, Planet Zoldath's fictional developer, and mechanics generating story (Into Ruins' missing stairs and Wings of Yendor, Brough's loadout story, Savant on altering input to express inner struggle, and its risks). Include Lait's experiments with endings and world decay as cautionary cases (a hidden ending nobody found), Banished Vault's target emotions, Hades-style tying of story progress to combat, rituals that give reasons to read. Note frictions: Qud's day length clashing with prose (Ivy Melinda). Close on Keenan's and Iseli's case that story should be optional yet supply goals and help newcomers, with guidance for checking that a mechanic and its fiction say the same thing.

sections.heading: What your systems say about your world
sections.brief: Argue Xalavier Nelson Jr.'s claim that generation systems, statistics and base numbers say more about a world than its writing: what counts as an organ, whether the soul is sellable, how stats advertise real weapons. Converge with Mendoza on shop prices as compressed signals of world events (Pathologic) and the worldbuilding commitment of a dungeon shopkeeper, Freeman on randomised tech trees implying a universe, procedural rhetoric in mechanics nobody intended, and Ray's reading of Qud's grid and ASCII abstractions as a bardic, unreliable telling. Add Cook's point that generated mechanics need a theme that explains the unknown, Harris's prediction of exploitable generated backstories, and depth as time. End with guidance: audit your numbers and generators for the worldview they encode, and use them deliberately to tell players about the world.

sections.heading: Setting a tone and holding it
sections.brief: Build around Jim Shepard's Dungeonmans talk: plot reference works on axes of humour, heroism and lore to pick a tone target, then use it as a razor for every line; deliver tone as comfortable background rather than in the player's face; beware abrupt shifts to dark drama. Then his humour rules (references invisible to those who miss them, play to your strengths, avoid edgy humour, playtest jokes) with name juxtaposition (Zack Johnson) and Alphaman's parody castles as examples. Set against this Blaseball's tone growing from community response (Clark), Dean's drumming metaphor for how much to write, and Julian Day's deliberate poetic touches widening a game's tone. End with a short method for defining and enforcing tone.

sections.heading: Choosing a setting and theme
sections.brief: Argue that setting is a design lever, not decoration: Josh Ge on unique non-fantasy themes as a source of mechanics, Carney's 'key and notes' where shared setting lets generated content cohere, Zapata on XRLs adapting existing worlds, and Coleman's trade-off that fantasy supplies familiarity for free while sci-fi needs 'narrative greebles'. Cover believable, coherent worlds (Biskup's ADOM, Qud's obscured Gamma World past, ADOM's static/procedural balance and Ultimate ADOM's multiverse and factions, Phillip Daigle on writing lore you genuinely care about). Then bounded and strange spaces: Pipkin on islands, enclosures and descent, the dungeon as heterotopia, theme carried by structure (Kiss Garden, Blaseball's broken rules), and interface games whose setting is the player's own screen (blekkenhorst). End with questions for picking a setting that generates play.

sections.heading: Writing the words: items, logs, dialogue and voice
sections.brief: Start with Julian Day's principle that how information is delivered builds the world, then Shepard's case against walls of text and for using the combat log, monster names and item descriptions as storytelling (Tangledeep's Mirai characterised through her gear, flavour text that does more than restate the item). Cover optional lore (Dean's bite-sized rewards in Pacific Drive, Elder Scrolls-style books that hide mandatory info) and brevity (Captain Blood's dying alien, Nuclear Throne's one-liners, Rogue-style short sentences). Then craft tools: narrative perspective, borrowed voices, dialogue that gives information first, translation workarounds, foreshadowing via proper nouns, twists built from small facts, audio logs, plot exposition fallbacks (Adams), generic systems with specific messages (Pepers). Finish with poetry and evocative prose in ADOM, Shadow of the Wyrm and Qud, including Day's stanza technique, and practical guidance for a writer's first pass.

sections.heading: Authored story inside a replayable structure
sections.brief: Frame the authoring problem: branching narratives explode (Junius, McHorse/Foster) and someone still has to write it all. Present Junius' braided narrative as the main answer (independent and shared conditions, Hades' run-based progression, varied gating, subset of cast per run, pacing caps of about three events per run, Three Houses' mutual supports) and note it still scales with scope. Converge with storylets and salience across Voyageur, Hintline 93 and Sunshine Shuffle, and related structures: Fallout board game consequence cards, Sea of Rifts with Ink, Dean's gating intro, 80 Days-style forward motion, Wolverson sequencing beats on the hot path. Include variations on fixed text with random order (Thompto, Neutrinowatch), content suspense (Pepers on Yakuza), hidden alternate endings, scripts bending to systemic objects (Wilson), and Reed's god's-eye multilinear view. End with a decision guide for picking a structure given team size and run length.

sections.heading: Procedural characters and a world that notices
sections.brief: Lead with Wildermyth (Belanger & Wagner, Brittain, McHorse/Foster): random generation leading into handcrafted content, acknowledging random misfortunes, adding variation wherever its absence would feel weird, per-personality voice splits, and the constraint that interchangeable heroes can't be caricatures; note the cheap trick of excluding events. Converge with Kreminski's procedural character arcs (reveal traits gradually, latent traits enabling foreshadowing, pre-generated best/worst endings, focus-weighted storylets, storylet chains) and his preference for simulationist over retroactive drama management. Add Reed's finding that relationship simulation pays off more than environmental detail, Brittain's argument that procedural casts break narrative hierarchies, culture-specific reference databases (Ultima Ratio Regum), Sloan's structural frameworks and map-linked names, and Compton's runtime-rewritten grammars. End with guidance for making generated characters feel authored.

sections.heading: Generated history and environmental storytelling
sections.brief: Show the convergent technique of generating a history and surfacing it as artefacts: Qud's sultans on shrines and painted amphoras, Dwarf Fortress engravings, Ivy Melinda on blind assembly leaving room for interpretation. Set Wehrle's Oath, which deliberately forgets and remembers selectively because gaps make history feel real, against full-record approaches. Cover ruins and interpretation: Nothing Beside Remains and role-based subjective descriptions (Smith Nicholls), Disco Elysium and Heaven's Vault, and La Horde du Contrevent's role-gated layers. Then the player-motivation problem: Lessard says accessible history doesn't make players care and builds a game role around it, Freeman says generated history is passive scenery unless playable, Otto warns long simulations are artefacts rather than spectacles, and Reed warns that simulation players don't notice is wasted (Blue Lacuna). End with guidance on scoping history generation to what players will encounter.

sections.heading: Finding and staging the drama
sections.brief: Argue the convergent point that a simulation's output is not yet a story: James Ryan's chronicle-sift-narrativize model via Kreminski, Bad News' wizard querying for latent drama, the SIBR speakers on logs and filtering signal from noise, and McHorse/Foster's warning that fluent connected information is not compelling narrative. Cover sifting as technique (pattern libraries, micro-stories, artificial commentators) and fidelity on demand. Then reality TV as a model for what to sift for and how to stage it: Greger's content hierarchy with raw emotion on top, the magic circle, party-of-rooms structure, constructed realities as dungeons (Leigh Alexander, including McMansion's shift to player-as-murderer), the confessional and the honesty of fakeness (Smith Nicholls), and statistics as at-a-glance stories (Blaseball). End with practical guidance for surfacing the best moments to players.

sections.heading: Generating plot: planners, quests and complications
sections.brief: Frame Stephen G. Ware's claim that the real problem is rewriting a story on the fly as a game master does, and that stories are non-Markovian, so quality is relative to alternatives. Set emergent agent stories (unpredictable, beats only hoped for) against planned ones (guaranteed requirements), with Kreminski's character-level and author-level goals and Otto's tit-for-tat factions as the failure that motivates planning; include Ware on intention, failed-plan explanations and replanning vs intervention. Then tabletop-derived methods: Capacle's surprise-with-coherence sweet spot and fail-forward complications (and their tendency to become repetitive), Savant's beginning/middle/end quest grammar with acceptance, triggers, struggles and returns. Add pacing by walking the social graph (Otto), layering and rapid change (Kiss Garden), Hidden Door's trope skeletons with LLM expression, puzzles' lack of story path (Alison), and Chekhov's gun in live play. End with guidance on choosing between simulation, planning and grammar approaches.

sections.heading: Borrowing responsibly: real symbols, cultures and the past
sections.brief: Argue that fiction built from real material carries real meaning: Stanley Baxton shows how 'real magic' symbols can make a game unknowingly antisemitic or appropriative, traces Western esoterica's appropriations, and gives tests (ask why, open vs closed traditions, avoid symbols with Hebrew letters) plus Fallen London as a good example. Pair with Cara Esten Hurtle on nostalgia, whose creative power is friction but which can wash over real harms, and Brough's case for engaging with dated fantasy to trace change. Include Nelson's call to own the perspective your game conveys, Thompto's spaces of contemplation that let minoritized creators resist single readings, and Leonhart's queer reading beyond representation. End with a short due-diligence routine for borrowed symbols and settings.
